name: Arithmetic mean
subject: statistics
description: Add the values and divide by how many there are.
meaning: Balance point of the data; sensitive to extreme values.
restrictions: Population mean is written \mu with the same arithmetic

example.problem: Six quiz scores are 7, 9, 6, 8, 10 and 8. Find the mean.
example.explanation: The sum of all values divided by the number of values.

verification.notes: OpenStax, Math is Fun worked example and definitions agree; population symbol mu vs sample x-bar only changes notation.

name: Mean from a frequency table / estimated mean of grouped data
subject: statistics
description: Multiply each value (or class midpoint) by its frequency, add, and divide by the total frequency.
meaning: Exact mean for a table of single values; an estimate for class intervals because individual values are unknown.

variables.name: frequency of the value or class

restrictions: For class intervals the result is an estimate only
derivation: Treating every value in a class as if it equalled the midpoint gives the weighted sum.

example.problem: Class midpoints and frequencies: 5→4, 15→6, 25→8, 35→2. Estimate the mean.
example.explanation: Each class is represented by its midpoint.

verification.notes: OpenStax (sum f*m / sum f) and Math is Fun (midpoint method, estimated mean) agree.

name: Range
subject: statistics
description: Largest value minus smallest value.
meaning: Simplest measure of spread; depends only on the two extreme values.
restrictions: Very sensitive to outliers

example.problem: Daily temperatures were 12, 18, 9, 22 and 15 degrees Celsius. Find the range.
example.explanation: Subtract the smallest from the largest.

verification.notes: OpenStax lists range among spread measures (chapter objective) but the fetched text does not spell out the subtraction; definition is elementary and was recomputed. Only one fetched source mentions it.

name: Percentile position (OpenStax convention)
subject: statistics
description: Find the position of the k-th percentile in ordered data of n values; average the two neighbours when i is not whole.
meaning: One of several percentile conventions; Q1 is k = 25, Q3 is k = 75.
conditions: If i is not an integer average the values at floor(i) and ceil(i) (as OpenStax describes)
restrictions: Other texts use k/100 × n or (n−1) with interpolation; results may differ

example.problem: For 11 sorted values, at which position is the 25th percentile under this convention?
example.explanation: Whole number, so Q1 is the third value.

verification.notes: OpenStax states this formula; MathWorld confirms multiple competing position conventions exist (e.g. (n+1)/4 for Minitab/Moore-McCabe) so no independent second statement of this exact formula beyond the (n+1)/4 equivalence for k = 25.

name: Interquartile range
subject: statistics
description: Distance between the third and first quartiles.
meaning: Width of the middle half of the data; resistant to extreme values.
conditions: Quartile method must be stated; different conventions can give different Q1, Q3
restrictions: Not the same as range

example.problem: A data set has Q1 = 5.5 and Q3 = 13.5. Find the IQR.

verification.notes: OpenStax, Math is Fun and MathWorld agree on IQR = Q3 - Q1; all three note or imply quartile convention dependence.

name: Outlier fences (1.5 × IQR rule)
subject: statistics
description: Values below the lower fence or above the upper fence are flagged as potential outliers.
meaning: A screening convention for unusually distant values; flagged points need investigation, not automatic removal.
restrictions: 1.5 is a convention; NIST also defines outer fences at 3 × IQR
Not a proof that a value is an error

example.problem: Q1 = 5 and Q3 = 9 for a data set. Find the upper fence.
example.explanation: Anything above 15 is a potential outlier.

verification.notes: OpenStax, NIST (twice) and MathWorld agree on the 1.5 × IQR fences; NIST adds the 3 × IQR outer fences.

name: Population variance
subject: statistics
description: Average of the squared distances from the population mean.
meaning: Use when the data are the whole population of interest (a census).
restrictions: Units are the square of the data units

example.problem: Data 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 are the entire population. Find the variance.

verification.notes: OpenStax (divide by N for population), MathWorld (sigma^2 as mean squared deviation) and Math is Fun agree.

name: Sample variance
subject: statistics
description: Add the squared distances from the sample mean and divide by n − 1.
meaning: Use when the data are a sample used to estimate a population's variance.
restrictions: Some sources/calculators use 1/n for 'sample variance'; MathWorld calls that the biased version
Check which convention your calculator uses (σx vs sx)
derivation: Dividing by n−1 (Bessel's correction) corrects the bias in estimating the population variance when the mean is estimated from the same data.

example.problem: Data 6, 8, 10, 12, 14 are a sample. Find the sample variance.
example.explanation: Same numerator as the population version but divided by 4, not 5.

verification.notes: OpenStax, MathWorld, Math is Fun agree on 1/(n-1); MathWorld explicitly documents the competing 1/N 'sample variance' and warns about notation. SRC-STP-056 is the same OpenStax text, not counted as independent.

name: Population standard deviation
subject: statistics
description: Square root of the population variance.
meaning: Typical distance from the mean, in the same units as the data.
restrictions: Zero only when all values are equal

example.problem: Find σ for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (population).

verification.notes: Sources agree: SD is the square root of variance; population version divides by N.

name: Sample standard deviation
subject: statistics
description: Square root of the sample variance.
meaning: Estimate of the population SD from sample data; the default on most calculators' 's' key.
restrictions: Not an unbiased estimator of σ even though s² is unbiased for σ²

example.problem: Find s for 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7, 9 (sample).

verification.notes: OpenStax and Math is Fun agree on n-1; Math is Fun's dog example (sd 147 population vs 165 sample) was recomputed independently.

name: z-score (standard score)
subject: statistics
description: How many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean.
meaning: Makes values from different distributions comparable.
restrictions: For a sample use x̄ and s
Percent interpretation needs an approximately normal distribution

example.problem: A score of 78 in a class with mean 70 and SD 4. Find z.

verification.notes: Math is Fun (explicit formula), LibreTexts pages (z-scores in normal-distribution sections) agree; no conflicts.

name: Least-squares slope
expression: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^{2}-\left(\sum x\right)^{2}}
subject: statistics
description: Slope of the line minimising the sum of squared vertical errors.
meaning: Predicted change in y for a one-unit increase in x.
restrictions: Valid for prediction inside the data range; extrapolation is risky

example.formula: b=\frac{n\sum xy-\sum x\sum y}{n\sum x^2-(\sum x)^2}

verification.notes: OpenStax gives the deviation form; Math is Fun and MathWorld give the sums form; recomputed numerically that both forms agree on the example.

name: Least-squares intercept
subject: statistics
description: The line passes through (x̄, ȳ), so the intercept is ȳ − b x̄.
meaning: Predicted y when x = 0 (meaningful only if x = 0 is realistic).
restrictions: Interpretation at x = 0 can be meaningless

example.problem: With slope 0.9, x̄ = 3, ȳ = 4 find a and predict y at x = 6.
example.explanation: x = 6 is just outside the data range, so treat with care.

verification.notes: OpenStax a = ȳ − b x̄; Math is Fun's intercept step from sums gives the same value on the checked example (b=0.9, a=1.3).

name: Pearson correlation coefficient (enrichment)
subject: statistics
description: Standardised measure of linear association between two variables.
meaning: Sign shows direction; |r| near 1 means points lie near a line; says nothing about causation.
conditions: At least two distinct values for each variable
restrictions: Measures linear association only
Sensitive to outliers
Correlation does not imply causation

example.problem: Using the five points (1,2),(2,3),(3,5),(4,4),(5,6), find r.

verification.notes: MathWorld gives r^2 = ss_xy^2/(ss_xx ss_yy) (sign from ss_xy); Math is Fun describes Pearson's correlation stepwise but its exact formula text was not captured, so the signed form is derived rather than copied. Enrichment topic.

name: Probability with equally likely outcomes
subject: probability
description: Count favourable outcomes and divide by the total number of equally likely outcomes.
meaning: Value between 0 (impossible) and 1 (certain).
restrictions: Not valid when outcomes have unequal chances

example.problem: Two fair dice are rolled. Find P(sum = 8).

verification.notes: OpenStax terminology and Math is Fun agree.

name: Complement rule
subject: probability
description: The chance A does not happen is 1 minus the chance it does.
meaning: Useful for 'at least one' questions.

example.problem: A bag has 4 red, 3 blue, 5 green marbles. Find P(not green).

verification.notes: OpenStax states P(A)+P(A')=1; Math is Fun uses 1 − P(no match) trick.

name: General addition rule
subject: probability
description: Add the probabilities, then subtract the overlap counted twice.
meaning: Probability that at least one of A or B occurs.

example.problem: 30 students: 18 play soccer, 12 play chess, 5 play both. Find P(soccer or chess).
example.explanation: Both-players were counted in each group.

verification.notes: OpenStax gives the probability form; MathWorld inclusion-exclusion gives the set-cardinality generalisation; consistent.

name: Addition rule for mutually exclusive events
subject: probability
description: If A and B cannot both happen, simply add.
meaning: Special case of the general rule where P(A ∩ B) = 0.
restrictions: Do not use when events overlap (e.g. King and Heart)

example.problem: One card from a deck: P(King or Queen).

verification.notes: OpenStax and Math is Fun agree.

name: Multiplication rule for independent events
subject: probability
description: Multiply the probabilities of independent events.
meaning: Also the test for independence.
restrictions: Not applicable without replacement unless re-computed as dependent

example.problem: Coin shows heads and a die shows 6.

verification.notes: OpenStax and Math is Fun agree.

name: General multiplication rule
subject: probability
description: Probability of A, times the probability of B given A happened.
meaning: Handles dependent events such as draws without replacement.

example.problem: Two cards drawn without replacement: both hearts.
example.explanation: Second draw has one fewer heart and one fewer card.

verification.notes: OpenStax, Math is Fun, MathWorld agree.

name: Conditional probability
subject: probability
description: Restrict attention to the outcomes where A occurred.
meaning: Updated probability of B given the information that A occurred.
restrictions: P(B|A) ≠ P(A|B) in general

example.problem: 80 students; 50 like pizza; 30 like pizza and pasta. Find P(pasta | pizza).

verification.notes: OpenStax, MathWorld, Math is Fun agree (MathWorld requires P(A)>0).

name: Law of total probability
subject: probability
description: Add the probabilities along all tree branches leading to B.
meaning: Splits an event across a partition A_1, …, A_n.
conditions: Union of A_i is the whole sample space

example.problem: Machine A makes 60% of items (2% defective); machine B 40% (5% defective). P(defective)?

verification.notes: MathWorld derives it within the Bayes proof; Math is Fun shows the tree-diagram version in a worked example, not a general statement.

name: Bayes' theorem
subject: probability
description: Reverse a conditional probability using the prior.
meaning: Updates belief in A after seeing B.
restrictions: Base rates matter

example.explanation: Most positives come from the large healthy group.

verification.notes: MathWorld, Math is Fun and MathWorld conditional-probability page give identical forms.

name: Expected value of a discrete random variable
subject: probability
description: Multiply each value by its probability and sum.
meaning: Long-run average.

example.problem: Win $10 (p 0.1), $2 (p 0.4), $0 (p 0.5); ticket $3. Expected net?

verification.notes: OpenStax, MathWorld, Math is Fun agree.

name: Fundamental counting principle
subject: probability
description: Multiply the number of choices at each stage.
meaning: Counts the ways to complete independent stages.
conditions: Number of choices at later stages not affected by earlier ones (or counted after adjustment)

example.problem: 4 shirts × 3 trousers × 2 pairs of shoes.

verification.notes: OpenStax Precalculus states the principle; Math is Fun shows repetition (n^r) as a special case, not as a general statement.

name: Factorial
subject: probability
description: Product of whole numbers from n down to 1.
meaning: Number of ways to arrange n distinct objects in a row.
restrictions: 0! = 1 by convention

example.problem: Compute 6!.

verification.notes: MathWorld and Math is Fun agree on n! as the product down to 1. The 0! = 1 convention was not located in the fetched text and is listed as a standard convention supported by reasoning only.

name: Permutations (ordered selections)
subject: probability
description: Number of ordered arrangements of r objects from n distinct objects.
meaning: Order matters; no repetition.

example.problem: Gold, silver, bronze among 8 runners.

verification.notes: MathWorld, Math is Fun and OpenStax agree.

name: Combinations (unordered selections)
subject: probability
description: Number of ways to choose r objects from n when order is irrelevant.
meaning: Divide permutations by r! to remove order.

example.problem: Committee of 3 from 10 students.
example.explanation: Each committee counted 3! = 6 times in permutations.

verification.notes: OpenStax, MathWorld (C(4,2)=6 example), Math is Fun agree.

name: Arrangements with repeated items
subject: probability
description: Divide n! by the factorial of each repeat count.
meaning: Counts distinct words/arrangements.

variables.name: number of identical items of type i

example.problem: Arrangements of STATISTICS (S×3, T×3, I×2, A, C).

verification.notes: Only one fetched source (OpenStax Precalculus, DISTINCT = 10,080) states it; recomputed 8!/(2!2!) = 10080.

name: Binomial probability
subject: probability
description: Probability of exactly k successes in n independent trials.
meaning: Counts which trials succeed (C(n,k)) times probability of each pattern.

example.problem: 5 free throws at p = 0.7. P(exactly 4)?

verification.notes: OpenStax, MathWorld, Math is Fun agree.

name: Mean of a binomial distribution
subject: probability
description: Expected successes in n trials.
meaning: Long-run average number of successes.

verification.notes: OpenStax and MathWorld (Np) agree.

name: Variance and SD of a binomial distribution
subject: probability
description: Spread of the number of successes.
meaning: Spread of the number of successes in n independent trials, where q = 1 − p; the mean is np and the variance npq.

verification.notes: Only OpenStax states npq explicitly among fetched pages; MathWorld page excerpt read gave the mean only.
